(p-213) (Sūrat Ṣād, Makkiyyah, and its verses are eighty-eight.)

﴿Ṣād﴾ is with a sukūn (vowelless) on account of pausing. It is also read with a kasrah and with a fatḥah, because of the meeting of two unvowelled letters (iltiqā' al-sākinayn). The fatḥah may be understood as the implied particle of oath in the position of a genitive, as in their saying: "Allāh, I will certainly do it" with the genitive (i.e., the oath particle is elided and the noun is in the genitive). It may also be that it is in the accusative by an implied verb, "remember" (udhkur) or "recite" (iqra'), not as a fatḥah as was mentioned at the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqarah. The non-declension (imtinā' al-ṣarf) is due to definiteness and femininity, since it is a proper name for the sūrah. Whoever reads it with tanwīn has declined it, treating it as the name of the Book or the Revelation. It has been said: in the reading with kasrah it is an imperative from al-muṣādāh (confronting, responding), which means opposition and confrontation, and from it comes the echo (al-ṣadā) that is reflected from solid bodies by the confrontation of sound. Its meaning: "Confront the Qur'ān with your action; so act by its commands, refrain from its prohibitions, and adorn yourself with its moral qualities." Then, if it is made the name of a letter arranged on the pattern of challenge, or a symbol pointing to a sentence such as "Allāh has spoken the truth" or "Muḥammad has spoken the truth," as has been transmitted from the great early scholars; or a name of the sūrah, as the predicate of an omitted subject; or in the accusative by an implied "remember" or "recite"; or an imperative from al-muṣādāh.

Then the "wāw" in His saying ﴿and the Qur'ān, full of reminder﴾ is for oath. If it is made the thing sworn by, then it is for conjunction with it. If by "the Qur'ān" is meant the whole of it, then the difference between them is real; if what is meant is the very sūrah, then it is a notional difference, as in your saying: "I passed by the generous man," and "by the blessed lineage." In any case, the repetition carries added emphasis on the content of the sentence sworn upon. "Dhikr" means nobility and distinction, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾, or it means admonition and exhortation, or the mention of what is needed in matters of religion, of laws and rulings and other things, such as the narratives of the prophets, peace be upon them, the reports of the past nations, and promise and threat.

The answer to the oath, according to the first, fourth and fifth aspects, is omitted; it is what the challenge, the command, and the swearing by it indicate, namely that the thing challenged is miraculous, that the thing commanded is obligatory, and that the thing sworn by deserves magnification. That is: "I swear by the Qur'ān," or "by Ṣād," that it is indeed miraculous, or that acting by it is obligatory, or that it truly deserves magnification. As for the remaining two aspects, the answer is the statement pointed to by the symbol. And the sentence itself mentioned before the oath: naming indicates the honour of the named and alerts to the greatness of its importance; that is: "Indeed, it is truthful, and by the Qur'ān full of reminder," or "this sūrah is of great significance, and by the Qur'ān...," following the pattern of their saying: "This is Ḥātim, by Allāh." Since each of these answers indicates the absence of doubt about its content entirely, there is an indication, while what His exalted saying was...

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 2:

﴿Nay, but those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition.﴾ This is a turning away (idrab) from that, as if it were said: there is no doubt about it, definitively. The disbelievers' failure to submit to it is not due to any admixture of doubt in it; rather, they are in great pride and zealous obstinacy, and in far-reaching opposition to Allah the Exalted and His Messenger, and for this reason they do not submit to it. (p-214) It was also said: the answer is what the idrabi sentence (al-jumlah al-idrabiyyah) indicates, i.e., that whoever disbelieved did so because of a flaw he found in it, rather [ceci: bal] "those who disbelieve..." etc. It has also been read as (fi ghirrah), i.e., in heedlessness regarding what it is obligatory for them to be alert to from the foundations of faith and its incentives.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 3:

﴿How many generations We destroyed before them!﴾ This is a warning to them for their disbelief and arrogance, by making clear what befell those arrogant ones who came before them. Kam (how many) is the object of "We destroyed" (ahlaknā), and min qarnin (of generations) is a specifier (tamyīz). The meaning is: "We destroyed many generations of the bygone centuries."

﴿Then they cried out﴾ when Our might descended and Our vengeance befell them, seeking help and repenting, so that they might be saved from that. The words of the Exalted, ﴿and there was no longer any time for escape﴾, form a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to the pronoun in "they cried out." That is: they cried out and sought help, seeking deliverance, while the reality was that the time was not a time of escape (manāṣ), meaning flight and deliverance from it. Here manāṣ is from nāṣa-hu, i.e., "he escaped from him," not from nāṣa meaning "he delayed." And lā here is not the lā that is made to work like laysa (the one that resembles laysa); rather the tā' of feminine marking was added to it for emphasis, just as it was added to rubba and thumma, and it is specifically used for negating times. Only one of its two complements appears, and most often its subject is omitted. It was also said that lā is the negation of the genus (nāfiyat li-l-jins) with the tā' added to it, and it is specifically used for negating times. "Ḥīna manāṣin" is in the accusative, taken as its subject, i.e., "and there is no time of escape for them," or it is governed by a suppressed verb, i.e., "and I see no time of escape." It was also read in the nominative. On the first reading, it is its subject and the predicate is omitted, i.e., "and there is no time of escape attained by them." On the second, it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, i.e., "and no time of escape belongs to them." It was also read in the genitive, as in the verse of the poet:

*They sought peace with us, but it was not a time for it,*
*so we answered that it was not a time for survival.*

Either because lāt governs times in the way that law-lā governs pronouns, as in the verse:

*Had it not been for you, I would not have made the pilgrimage this year.*

Or because awān (time) was likened to idh in the verse of the poet:

*I forbade you from pursuing Umm 'Amr, while you were healthy in wellbeing...*

in that it is a time from which the genitive complement was cut off and tanwīn was substituted for it, since its original form is "awān ṣulḥ" (time of peace). Then ḥīn manāṣ was modeled on it, treating the cutting off of the complement from manāṣ as analogous to cutting it from ḥīn, because of the unity between the two genitive constructions. Then ḥīn was indeclinable because it was attached to a non-declinable noun. It was also read "lāti" with a kasra like "jayr." The Kufans stop on it with a hā' as with nouns, and the Basrans with a tā' as with verbs. As for what has been said, that the tā' is added to ḥīn because it is joined to it in the Imam (the master copy of the Qur'an), this has no basis, for the orthography of the codex lies outside analogy.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 4:

﴿And they marvel that a warner has come to them from among themselves.﴾ This is a recounting of their falsehoods, which branch off from what has been related of their arrogance and opposition; that is: they marvel that a messenger of their own kind has come to them, and moreover one lower than them in worldly leadership. The meaning is that they regarded this as a strange matter, outside the realm of possibility, and denied it in the strongest terms, not that they believed it had occurred and were amazed by it.

﴿And the disbelievers say﴾ The apparent noun is placed where the pronoun would be, in anger at them and as a notice that none would dare to say the like of what they say except those who go deep into disbelief and wickedness.

﴿This is a sorcerer﴾ in what he displays of extraordinary acts, ﴿a liar﴾ in what he attributes to Allah the Exalted regarding sending and sending down.

﴿Has He made the gods one God?﴾ That is, by denying divinity to them and restricting it to one.

﴿Indeed, this is a thing to be wondered at.﴾ Extremely astonishing. This is because it contradicts what their fathers, upon whom they agreed in regarding them as gods and whom they persistently worshipped, had established, generation after generation. For this (imitation of forefathers) is the basis of everything they do or leave undone in matters of their religion: it is taqlid (blind imitation) and habit. So they regard whatever contradicts what they are accustomed to as strange, even impossible. As for making the basis of their astonishment the failure of one god's knowledge and power to encompass many things, there is no justification for this, since they do not claim that their gods have knowledge, power, or any role in the occurrence of anything, such that denying their divinity would entail that effects remain without an agent.

It has been read as ʿajjāb (عَجّاب) with shaddah (emphatic doubling), which is more intensive, like kirām and karrām (كَرام and كَرّام). It is narrated that when ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, embraced Islam, this grieved the Quraysh, and twenty-five of their chieftains gathered and came to Abu Talib and said: "You are our elder and our chief, and you know what these foolish ones have done. We have come to you so that you may judge between us and your nephew." So he summoned the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O my nephew, these are your people, and they are asking you a request, so do not incline entirely away from your people." He (ﷺ) said: "What do you ask of me?" They said: "We will abandon [our opposition], and you abandon the mention of our gods, and we will leave you and your God." He (ﷺ) said: "Tell me, if I grant you what you ask, will you give me one word by which you will rule the Arabs and by which non-Arabs will submit to you?" They said: "Yes, and ten [such words]." He said: "Say: There is no god but Allah." So they stood up and said it.

**Abu al-Su'ud, *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*, on Surah 38, verse 6:**

﴿And the chiefs among them went away﴾, i.e., the nobles of Quraysh departed from the assembly of Abu Talib after the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had silenced them with a ready and decisive reply. They witnessed his steadfastness (ﷺ) in the religion and his resolve to make it prevail over all religion, and they despaired of what they had been hoping for through the mediation of Abu Talib, namely a compromise on the aforementioned terms.

﴿"Walk on"﴾, i.e., saying to one another, out of sincere advice: "Walk on."

﴿"And be steadfast for your gods"﴾, i.e., persist in worshipping them, bearing patiently what you hear of disparagement concerning them. The particle *an* (أن) here is explanatory (*al-mufassira*), because departing from a gathering of mutual talk does not occur without speech. It has also been said that the meaning of "departing" is "rushing forth into speech." *Imshu* (امشوا) derives from *mashat al-mar'atu*, when a woman bears many children, and from it comes *al-mashiya* (the livestock), by way of optimism (*al-tafa'ul*), i.e., "gather together and multiply." It was also read *imshu* without *an*, with the verb of saying implied (*idmar al-qawl*). It was also read *yamshuna an isbiru* (يمشون أن اصبروا).

﴿"Indeed this is a thing intended"﴾ is a justification for the command to be steadfast, or for the obligation to comply with it. That is: this which we have witnessed from Muhammad (ﷺ), concerning the matter of monotheism, the negation of our gods, and the nullification of their cause, is a thing intended, i.e., on his part (ﷺ) its execution and implementation is inevitable, without any deterrent that turns him aside or any inclination that bends him, not a mere statement uttered by the tongue, nor a matter in which leniency may be hoped for through intercession or favour. So cut off your hopes of bringing him down from his opinion through the mediation and intercession of Abu Talib. It is enough for you that you are not wholly prevented from worshipping your gods; so be steadfast in them, and bear what you hear of disparagement and ill speech concerning them.

It has also been said: this matter is a thing God Most High intends, and He decrees its execution, and what God intends to bring about cannot be repelled, and nothing avails against it except patience. It has been said: this matter is one of the calamities of time that is intended against us, so there is no escape for us from it. It has been said: your religion is a thing sought (*yurad*), i.e., it is pursued in order to be taken from you, and you are overcome by it. It has been said: what he claims of monotheism, or what he aims at of leadership and of exalting himself over Arabs and non-Arabs, is a thing desired, which everyone wishes for. So reflect on these sayings, and choose from among them what the sublime composition (*al-nazm al-jalil*) supports.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 7:

﴿We have not heard of this﴾ which he says.

﴿in the last religion﴾ i.e., the Christian religion, which is the last of the religions, for they are Trinitarian; or in the religion upon which we found our fathers (p-216). It is also permissible for the prepositional phrase to be a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to ﴿this﴾, meaning: "We have not heard of this from the People of the Book or the soothsayers, existing in the awaited religion." And they lied in that the most abominable lie, for the report of the mission (ba'tha) and of monotheism (tawhid) was the most widely known of matters before the manifestation (of the Prophet).

﴿This is not﴾ i.e., this is nothing but.

﴿except a fabrication﴾ i.e., a lie that he invented.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 8:

﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him, out of all of us?﴾ That is: the Qur'an.

﴿Out of all of us?﴾ Meaning: while we are the chiefs of the people and their nobles. This is like their saying: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two cities?﴾ Their intention is to deny that it is a reminder sent down from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, just as their saying: ﴿Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it.﴾ Such false statements are evidence that the basis of their denial is nothing but envy and a narrow focus on worldly trash.

﴿Rather, they are in doubt about My Reminder.﴾ That is: about the Qur'an, or the revelation, because they incline to blind imitation and turn away from reflecting on the proofs that lead to knowledge of its truth. Their creed contains nothing on which they can make a firm decision, so they are wavering among illusions, attributing it at one time to sorcery and at another time to fabrication.

﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment.﴾ That is: rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment. When they taste it, the true reality will become clear to them. The word "lamma" indicates that their tasting is about to occur, and the meaning is that they will not believe in it until the punishment touches them. It has also been said: they have not tasted My punishment promised in the Qur'an, and for this reason they doubt it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 9:

﴿Or do they have the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord, the Mighty, the Bestower?﴾ Rather, do they have the treasuries of His mercy, exalted is He, so that they dispose of them as they wish, to bestow them upon whomever they will, withhold them from whomever they will, and exercise authority over them according to the dictates of their opinions, choosing for prophethood some of their chieftains (ṣanādīd). The meaning is that prophethood is a gift from Allah, mighty and majestic is He, which He bestows by His grace upon whomever He wills of His chosen servants, with none to prevent Him, for He is al-ʿAzīz (the Mighty), i.e., the Dominant who is not overcome, al-Wahhāb (the Bestower), who has the right to grant everything He wills to everyone He wills. In attributing the name of the Lord (al-Rabb), which indicates nurturing and bringing [His message] to perfection, to his pronoun (ﷺ), there is an honouring of him (ﷺ) and a kindness to him that is not hidden. And His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 10:

﴿Or do they have the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them?﴾ This is a reinforcement (tarshih) of what preceded, meaning: rather, do they have dominion over these upper and lower worlds, so that they may speak about divine affairs and exercise control over the divine arrangements which the Lord of Might and Majesty alone holds exclusively? The words of the Exalted: ﴿Then let them ascend by the means﴾ are the response to an omitted conditional clause (jawab shart mahdhuf), meaning: if they indeed possess the dominion mentioned, then let them climb by the ascents and pathways (al-ma'arij wa'l-manahij) through which one reaches the Throne, so that they may settle upon it, manage the affairs of the world, and send down revelation to whomever they choose and deem fitting. In this there is such mockery of them that there is no limit beyond it. The word sabab (means) in its basic sense is a connection (al-wasla). It was said: the intended meaning of "asbab" is the heavens, because they are the causes (asbab) of lower events; and it was said: their gates (abwabuha).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 11:

﴿A host, here, defeated, of the factions.﴾ That is: they are a host of disbelievers, banding together against the Messengers, who will shortly be defeated and broken. So do not concern yourself with what they say, nor be troubled by what they babble. The "mā" (ما) is superfluous, for the sake of diminishing and belittling, like your saying: "I ate something (شيئًا ما)." It has also been said that it is for magnification, as in mockery. "Here" (هنالك) indicates the place where they placed themselves by undertaking such a monstrous saying. And His, exalted is He, statement:

Qur'an 38:12: "Before them the people of Noah, and 'Ad, and Pharaoh, the lord of stakes, denied [their messengers]..." ... etc.

This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) confirming the content of what precedes it, by explaining the condition of these tyrants and transgressors, who are the army of those (before them); none of their hosts is spared from what they did of denial, nor from the punishment inflicted upon them. "Dhu al-Awtad" means "the possessor of firm dominion." Its origin is the firmness of a tent that is pitched with stakes (awtad), and so it is used metaphorically for the stability of kingship, the entrenchment of sovereignty, and the soundness of affairs. Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur said:

"And indeed they lived therein in the most pleasant of lives, in the shade of a kingdom whose stakes were firm."

Or it means "the possessor of large hosts," so called because some of them bind others together as a stake binds a building. It is also said: he set up four poles, and he would stretch the hands and feet of the one being tortured toward them, drive stakes into them, and leave him until he died. It is also said: he would stretch him between four stakes in the ground and let loose upon him punishments and serpents. And it is said: he had stakes and cords with which he would play before himself.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 13:

﴿And Thamud, and the people of Lot, and the companions of the Thicket﴾ The companions of the Thicket (al-aykah) are the people of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the factions﴾ may be an apposition (badal) to the groups mentioned, just as that Book (dhalika al-kitab) is an apposition to "Alif Lam Mim" according to one of the readings. In it there is an emphasis (fadl ta'kid) and an alert (tanbih) that they are the ones from whom the defeated army was made up. And His saying, exalted is He:

[Indeed, none of them but denied the Messengers] is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*) brought in to affirm their denial, to explain its manner, and to prepare for what follows. That is: no single individual from those factions, nor the factions themselves, nor any group among them, did anything but deny the Messengers, because the denial of one of them is a denial of all of them, since they all agree upon the truth. It has been said: no group among them did anything but deny its messenger, in the manner of matching a plural with a plural. Whichever is the case, the exception is an incomplete exclusive construction (*istithna' mufarragh*) drawn from the most general of the causal attributes in the predicate of the subject. The meaning is: no one of them is subject to any judgment except that he is judged as having denied the Messengers. It has been said: no one of them is the subject of any report except that he is reported as having denied the Messengers.

In attributing the denial to the groups mentioned, first in an indefinite manner, second by indicating that each of them is a distinct faction that banded together against its messenger, and third by clarifying the manner of their denial through the exceptive sentence, there are various forms of emphasis (*funun min al-mubalaghah*) recording against them that they deserve the most severe and dreadful punishment. For this reason the words of Allah the Exalted follow: ﴿So My punishment became due﴾. That is: My punishment, which their crimes necessitated, of the kinds of penalties detailed in their proper places, was established and befell each one of them. Or it is with the subject (*al-mubtada'*). The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, none of them but denied the Messengers﴾, have their predicate with the returning pronoun omitted, meaning: indeed, each of them... etc. The sentence is a resumptive sentence that confirms what precedes it and reinforces its content, together with the explanation of the manner of their denial and the indication that they are the ones whom the defeated army was drawn from, as mentioned. It has been said: it is a subject and predicate. The meaning is that the factions from whom the defeated army was formed are themselves the ones, and that they are the ones from whom denial was found, so reflect upon this. As for what has been said, that the predicate is the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿and ʿĀd﴾... etc., or His words, ﴿and the people of Lot﴾... etc., such a view must be kept far from the sanctity of the revelation.

(p-218) ﴿Wa-ma yanzuru hA'ulA'i﴾ (And these [people] await nothing) begins the explanation of the punishment of the Makkan unbelievers, following the explanation of the punishment of their counterparts among the confederates (al-ahzab), who were told earlier that they were a contemptible host, routed soon. That in itself necessarily makes the listener expect and anticipate the explanation, with certainty. The use of "these" (hA'ulA'i) to refer to them conveys belittling of their status and making light of their affair. As for taking it to refer to the confederates in terms of their presence in the mention, or their presence in the knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, this is not within the realm of possibility at all. How could it be otherwise, since waiting, whether real or mocking, is only conceivable with regard to someone on whose deeds their consequences have not yet been brought about? And after he had explained the punishment of the confederates and their complete annihilation, nothing remained of what was intended to be explained of their punishments that was still awaited. Rather, those who are in the position of waiting are the Makkan unbelievers, who have committed among the greatest crimes and gravest sins that call for the most severe punishments, like what the confederates committed or worse, and who have not yet encountered any of its calamities. That is: "And these unbelievers, who are like those destroyed groups in unbelief and denial, await nothing."

﴿Illa sayhatan wahidatan﴾ (except a single blast): it is the second blast (al-nafkha al-thaniya), not in the sense that their punishment is itself that blast with its severity and terror, for it is a calamity whose terror encompasses all nations, the righteous and the wicked alike. Rather, it means that between them and the arrival of the dreadful punishment prepared for them there is nothing but it, since their punishment is deferred to the Hereafter, because their torment by annihilation is according to what they deserve. The Prophet (ﷺ) was among them, outside the divine custom founded on manifest wisdom, as indicated by the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾. As for what has been said, that it is the first blast, this has no basis at all, because its terror is not witnessed, and no one is struck senseless by it except one who was alive at the time of its occurrence; and their promised punishment does not occur right after it, nor is the general punishment deferred until then; rather it befalls them from the moment of their death.

﴿Ma lahA min fawaq﴾ (it will have no respite): that is, no pause of the length of a fawaq, which is the interval between two milkings. It is also read with a dammah on the fa', and both are dialectal forms (lughatan). And the words of Allah, Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 16:

﴿And they said: "Our Lord, hasten for us our share (qitt) before the Day of Reckoning."﴾ This is a report of what they said upon hearing that their punishment had been deferred to the Hereafter. That is, they said, by way of mockery and derision: "Hasten for us our qitt of the punishment with which You threaten us, and do not defer it until the Day of Reckoning, whose beginning is the Blast mentioned above." Al-qitt (the portion, the share) is a piece of something, from qatta-hu, when one cuts it off. It is also said that a writ of reward is called qitt, because it is a piece of paper, and it has been explained in this sense; that is, "Hasten for us the record of our deeds, that we may look into it." It has also been said: when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ mentioned Allah Most High's promise to the believers of Paradise, they said, mocking him: "Hasten for us our share of it." The opening of their supplication with the aforementioned address (nida') is for the sake of intensifying the mockery, as if they were calling for that with complete desire and entreaty.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 17:

﴿Be patient over what they say﴾, [bearing with] such false sayings as these.

﴿And remember﴾ for them ﴿Our servant Dawud﴾, i.e., his story, to magnify the matter of disobedience in their eyes and to alert them to the utmost ugliness of the sins they have dared to commit. For he (ﷺ), despite the loftiness of his station and his being singled out for great blessings and honors, when he was afflicted by a minor sin, he came down from his rank, and the angels rebuked him through allegory and allusion until he became aware, sought forgiveness from his Lord, and turned penitently to Him. There came from him what is related of his unceasing weeping, his enduring grief, and his constant remorse. So what, then, is to be supposed of these disbelievers, the most abject of all the abject, who commit the greatest of major sins and persist in the most grievous of transgressions?! Or, remember his story, peace be upon him, and guard yourself against slipping in what you have been charged with, namely enduring them and bearing their harm, lest there befall you what befell him of reproach.

﴿Dha al-Ayd﴾, i.e., possessor of strength. It is said: "Fulan ayd" and "dhu ayd," and "ad" has the same meaning, and "ayad" of everything is that by which it is strengthened.

﴿Indeed he was awwab﴾, one who returns repeatedly to the pleasure of Allah the Exalted. This is a justification for his being dha al-ayd, and an indication that what is meant by it is strength in religion, for he (peace be upon him) used to fast one day and break his fast the next day, and would stand in prayer for half the night.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 18:

﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] along with him﴾ This is a resumptive clause, brought to explain his strength in religion and his turning often (awwabiyyah) to what pleases Allah, exalted is He. The phrase "ma'a" (along with) is connected to the subjecting (taskhir), and its choice over the preposition "li" (for) is due to what was indicated in Surah al-Anbiya' (ئ), that the subjection of the mountains to him, upon him be blessings and peace, was not by way of entrusting full disposal over them to him, upon him be blessings and peace, as with the subjection of the wind and other things to Sulayman, upon him be peace; rather, it was by way of following him, upon him be blessings and peace, and emulating him in the worship of Allah, exalted is He. It has also been said that it is connected to what follows it, and this is closer, with regard to what is in Surah al-Anbiya', upon them all be blessings and peace.

﴿glorifying﴾ meaning: sanctifying Allah, mighty and majestic, with a voice that takes a form perceptible to him, or by Allah, exalted is He, creating speech in them, or by the tongue of their state (lisan al-hal). It has been said: they traverse with him by swimming (min al-sibahah), and this is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the mountains," placed in the position of "glorifying ones" to indicate the renewal of glorification state after state; and it is a resumptive clause clarifying the manner of the subjection.

﴿at evening and at ishraq﴾ meaning: and at the time of ishraq (ishraq, the sun's brightening), which is when the sun shines (tushriq), i.e., it lights up and its rays become clear; this is the time of forenoon (duha). As for its shuruq, it is its rising (tuloo'). It is said: "The sun has shone (shariqat) but has not yet ishraq (tushriq)." It is narrated from Umm Hani, may Allah be pleased with her, that "he, upon him be blessings and peace, prayed the forenoon prayer and said: 'This is the prayer of ishraq.'" And it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said: "I did not know the forenoon prayer except through this verse."

﴿And the birds﴾ is in apposition to (conjoined with) "the mountains." ﴿Mustahshara﴾ (gathered together) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "the birds," and the governing verb is "We subjected" (sakharnā), meaning: and We subjected the birds, in the state of being gathered together. From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: whenever (Dawud) glorified Allah, the mountains would respond to him with glorification, and the birds would gather around him and glorify (Allah) too, and that is their gathering (ḥashr). It has also been read as ﴿wa-l-ṭayru maḥshūratun﴾ (with the birds in the nominative), as a beginning (mubtada') and predicate (khabar).

﴿Each one of them is oft-returning (awwāb) to Him﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnāf) that confirms the meaning of what precedes it, explicitly stating what was understood in general terms from the glorification of the birds. That is: each one of the mountains and the birds, on account of His glorification, is returning (rajjāʿ) to glorification. The word awwāb is placed in the position of "one who glorifies" (musabbiḥ), either because they used to repeat the glorification (turajjiʿu al-tasbīḥ), and one who repeats it is a rajjāʿ, since he returns to his act again and again; or because awwāb means one who turns repeatedly to Allah, the Exalted, and whose habit is to increase remembrance and persist in glorifying and sanctifying (Him). It has also been said: the pronoun refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, meaning: each of Dawud, the mountains, and the birds is awwāb to Allah, that is, glorifying and repeating the glorification.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 20:

﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾ We strengthened it with awe, with victory, and with a great number of soldiers. It is also read with the doubled consonant (shaddah), *shaddadna*, for emphasis. It is said: forty thousand armed men would spend the night around his prayer niche (mihrab). It is also said: a man brought a claim against another concerning a cow, and he was unable to establish proof. God the Exalted revealed to him in a dream that he should kill the defendant. He delayed, so the revelation was repeated while he was awake, and he informed the man. The man said: "God the Exalted did not seize me for this sin, but for the fact that I killed the father of this one by treachery (*ghilah*)." The people said: "If anyone commits a sin, God the Exalted will expose it and have him killed for it." So they stood in awe of him, and his awe grew in their hearts.

﴿And We gave him wisdom﴾ meaning prophethood, perfection of knowledge, and excellence in action. It is also said: the Psalms (*Zabur*) and knowledge of the laws. It is also said: every speech that agrees with the truth is wisdom.

﴿And decisive speech (fasl al-khitab)﴾ that is, the decisive judgment in a dispute, by distinguishing truth from falsehood. Or it is a concise speech that alerts the addressee to the intended meaning without ambiguity, having observed the appropriate places for separation and connection, conjunction and resumption, explicit and implicit reference, omission and repetition. It is for this reason that *amma ba'du* ("as for what follows") is so called, because it separates the intended matter from what preceded it, as a preface to it, like praise (*hamd*) and blessing (*salah*). It is also said: it is decisive speech that contains neither damaging brevity nor tedious prolixity, as was said in describing the speech of prophethood: "decisive, neither sparse nor frivolous."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 21:

﴿Has the news of the litigants reached you?﴾ This is an interrogative whose meaning is amazement and eagerness to hear what follows it, indicating that it is among the wondrous news which ought to spread among every present and absent person. Al-khasm (the litigant, adversary) is originally a verbal noun (masdar), and for this reason it is applied to the one and to more than one, like al-dayf (the guest). The meaning of khasman (two litigants) is two parties.

﴿when they climbed over the sanctuary wall﴾ i.e., when they ascended its wall (suwr) and descended to him. The suwr is the high wall. Its parallel is tasannamahu, when he rose to its hump (sanam), and tadharrahu, when he rose to its summit (dhirwah). The "idh" (when) is connected to an omitted element, i.e., "the news of the litigants' dispute when they climbed over," or to "the news," on the understanding that what is meant is the event that occurred in the time of Dawud (peace be upon him), and that its attribution of "coming" to it is by omission of a modifier, i.e., "the story of the news of the litigants," or to "the litigants" because of what it contains of the meaning of contention; not to "atā" (came), because his coming to the Messenger (ﷺ) did not take place at that time. And His, the Exalted's, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 22:

﴿When they entered upon Dawud﴾ is a substitute (badal) for what precedes it, or an adverbial clause (zarf) governed by ﴿they scaled the wall﴾ (tasawwaru).

﴿So he was startled by them﴾. It is narrated that Allah, exalted is He, sent to him two angels in the form of two men. It is said: they were Jibril and Mika'il, peace be upon them both. They asked to enter upon him, but they found him on his day of worship, and the guards prevented them. So they scaled the prayer niche (mihrab) over him, together with the angels who were with them, and he did not perceive them until they were sitting before him, and so he was startled by them, because they had descended upon him from above, contrary to custom, while the guards were around him on a day other than the day of judgment and adjudication. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: Dawud, peace be upon him, divided his time into four parts: one day for worship, one day for judgment, one day for attending to his own personal affairs, and one day for admonition and reminder.

﴿They said﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that came as an answer to a question arising from the report of his fright, peace and blessings be upon him, as if it were said: What did the angels say when they witnessed his fright? So it is said: They said, to remove his fear.

﴿Fear not. We are two adversaries﴾, that is: we are two groups in dispute, applying the term "adversary" to a companion of the adversary.

﴿One of us has wronged the other﴾. This is on the basis of supposition and the intent of confrontation, so there is no lie in it.

﴿So judge between us with truth and do not exceed (tushtit) [the bounds]﴾, that is: do not deviate (la tajur) in judgment. It has also been read as (wa la tashtut), meaning: do not stray far from the truth. It has also been read as (wa la tushatit). All of these derive from the meaning of shatat (shatat), which is going beyond the limit and transgressing the truth.

﴿And guide us to the even path (sawa' al-sirat)﴾, that is: to the middle of the way of truth, by restraining the transgressor from the path of injustice he has taken, and guiding him to the course of justice.

(p-221) ﴿Indeed, this is my brother﴾ — a resumptive clause explaining what the dispute concerns, namely: my brother in religion, or in companionship. Mentioning this serves as a preface to showing how utterly ugly was what his companion did to him.

﴿He has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe﴾ — the ewe (našāt) is the female of sheep (ḍaʾn), and it may be used as a metaphor for a woman; allusion and indirect speech are more eloquent in purpose. It has also been read as ﴿tis‘un wa-tis‘ūna﴾ with a fatḥah on the tāʾ, and ﴿niʿjah﴾ with a kasrah on the nūn. It has also been read as ﴿wa-liya naʿjah﴾ with the yāʾ sukūn.

﴿So he said, "Entrust her to me"﴾ — i.e., make her mine (malliknīhā). Its literal sense is: make me responsible for her (akfulahā) as I am responsible for what is under my hand. It has also been said: make her my portion (kifl), i.e., my share.

﴿And he overpowered me in speech﴾ — i.e., he got the better of me in addressing me in argument, by bringing a contention I could not refute; or in contending against me in the proposal (al-khiṭbah). One says: "I proposed to the woman (khaṭabtu al-mar'ah), and he proposed to her (khaṭabahā huwa), so he addressed me with an address (fa-khāṭabanī khiṭāban)," meaning he overcame me in the proposal, so he prevailed over me by marrying her without me. It has also been read as ﴿wa-ʿāzzanī﴾, meaning he overcame me; and ʿazzanī with the zāy lightened, seeking lightness — a rare lightening, as if it were analogized to ẓaltu and mastu.

﴿He said, "He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe be added to his ewes."﴾ This is the answer to an omitted oath. By it, upon him be peace, he intended to emphasize his denunciation of his companion's act and to disparage his greed for the ewe of one who has no other, although he himself has a flock of them. Perhaps upon him be peace said this after his companion acknowledged what he had claimed against him, or he based it on assuming the claimant to be truthful. The word *as-su'al* ("demanding") is a verbal noun (*masdar*) annexed to its object, and its transitivity to a second object by means of *ila* ("to") is because it carries the sense of addition and joining.

﴿And indeed many of the partners﴾, meaning the associates who have mixed their property, ﴿transgress﴾, meaning they act unjustly. It is also read with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, on the assumption of a light *nun* that is then dropped, and with the *ya'* dropped, relying on the *kasra* (as a sign of the omitted letter).

﴿some of them against others﴾, not observing the right of companionship and partnership.

﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ among them, for they guard themselves against transgression and aggression. ﴿And few are they﴾, meaning: and they are few. The *ma* here is a redundant particle (*zā'idah*), used for vagueness and to express amazement at their scarcity, and the sentence is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tirāḍ*).

﴿And David thought that We had only tried him﴾. The verb *zann* ("thought") is used metaphorically for inferential knowledge, because of the apparent resemblance between them. That is, he came to know what had taken place in the session of judgment. It has been said that when he had passed judgment between them, one of them looked at his companion and laughed, then they both ascended to the sky in front of his face, and upon him be peace knew that He, the Exalted, had tested him. The meaning does not restrict the trial to him, upon him be peace, to the exclusion of others, by directing the restriction (*qaṣr*) conveyed by the word *innamā* to the object in comparison with another object, as is the common usage that directs restriction to the components and conditions of the verb, by considering negation in it and affirmation in them, as in the example of your saying, "I only struck Zayd," and "My striking him was for discipline." Rather, the meaning restricts his condition, upon him be peace, to the trial, by directing the restriction to the act itself in comparison with other acts differing from it, but not by considering negation and affirmation together regarding the particular nature of the act, for that is certainly impossible. Rather, it is by considering negation in what it contains of the general meaning of the act, and affirmation in what accompanies it of the specific meaning. For every specific act, on close examination, resolves into a general meaning, which is the signification of the word of the verb, and into a specific meaning which accompanies it and qualifies it, and which is its actual effect. For the meaning of *naṣara* ("he helped") is, for example, "he performed helping." This is indicated by the saying, "So-and-so gives and withholds," meaning, "he performs giving and withholding." Thus the true locus of the restriction is what relates to the act, by considering negation in it and affirmation in what relates to it. So the meaning is: "And David, upon him be peace, knew that We had only caused him trial." It has been said: We tested him with the wife of Uriah. It has also been said: We examined him with that judgment, to see whether he would be alerted by it to what was intended by it. The choice of the method of allegory is because it is more forceful in rebuke, for reflection on it, if it leads him to perceive the purpose, has a greater effect on his soul, a more powerful impact on his heart, and is more conducive to alerting him to the error, together with what it contains of observing his dignity, upon him be peace, by avoiding open reproach, and of indicating that it is a matter about which one is shy to speak plainly. Its depiction as a litigation was to compel him, upon him be peace, to state explicitly that he himself had done wrong, and to alert him, upon him be peace, to the fact that Uriah was about to dispute.

﴿So he sought forgiveness from his Lord﴾, immediately after it became known that what had proceeded from him was a sin, ﴿and fell down prostrate and turned penitently﴾. That is, he fell down in prostration, calling prostration "*rukū'*" (bowing) because it is its beginning. Or he fell down for prostration in the posture of bowing, meaning in prayer, as if he had entered into the state of ritual prayer with two *rak'ahs* of seeking forgiveness.

﴿And turned penitently﴾, meaning he returned to Allah, the Exalted, in repentance.

The essence of the story is that David, upon him be peace, saw the wife of a man called Uriah, his heart inclined toward her, and he asked him to divorce her. He was ashamed to refuse him, so he did so, and he married her. She was the mother of Solomon, upon him be peace. Such a thing was permissible in his law and customary among his people, not detracting from one's manliness, since they would ask one another to give up their wives to them so that they might marry them if they pleased them. In the early period of Islam the Helpers (*al-Anṣār*) would also share with the emigrants (*al-Muhājirūn*) in a similar manner without objection. Except that, because of the greatness of his station, the height of his rank, and the elevation of his status, upon him be peace, he was admonished through the allegory that it was not fitting for him to engage in what the ordinary individuals of his community engage in, namely asking a man who has only one wife to give her up so that he might marry her, despite his having many wives. Rather, it was obligatory for him to overcome his desire, to restrain his soul, and to be patient with what he had been tested with.

It has been said: Uriah had not married her; rather, he had proposed to her, then David, upon him be peace, proposed to her, and her family preferred him, upon him be peace. So his sin, upon him be peace, was that he proposed upon the proposal of his Muslim brother, and this is it.

As for what is mentioned, that upon him be peace entered his sanctuary one day, locked its door, and began to pray and recite the Psalms (*al-Zabūr*). While he was thus, the Devil came to him in the form of a golden dove, so he extended his hand to take it for a young son of his, but it flew away. He stretched toward it, and it flew away and fell into a window, so he followed it and saw a beautiful woman who had loosed her hair, so he covered her body. She was the wife of Uriah. And Uriah was on the expedition of al-Balqā'. He wrote to Ayyūb ibn Ṣūrīyā, who was the commander of the army of al-Balqā', "Send Uriah forward, and place him in front of the Ark." Whoever was placed in front of the Ark was not permitted to retreat until Allah granted victory at his hands or he was martyred. Allah, the Exalted, granted victory at his hand and he was safe, so he (David) ordered that he be sent back a second time, and a third time, until he was killed. The news of his death reached him, but he did not grieve as he would grieve over martyrs, and he married his wife. This is a fabricated lie, an invented fabrication, a most abominable falsehood that ears reject and natures recoil from. Woe to whoever invented it and spread it, and destruction to whoever fabricated it and disseminated it.

For this reason, Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Whoever narrates the story of David, upon him be peace, according to what the storytellers report, I will flog him one hundred and sixty times." This is the prescribed punishment for slander against the Prophets, may the blessings and peace of Allah, the Exalted, be upon them all.

It has also been said: A group intended to kill him, upon him be peace, so they scaled the sanctuary and entered upon him, and they found with him some people. They feigned this litigation. Upon him be peace understood their purpose, so he resolved to take revenge upon them. He thought that this was a trial from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so he sought forgiveness from his Lord for what he had resolved upon, and turned penitently.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 25:**

(p-223) ﴿So We forgave him that﴾, that is, what he sought forgiveness for. It is related that he, peace be upon him, remained prostrate for forty days and nights, not lifting his head except for the prescribed prayer (salah) or for what was unavoidable, and his tears did not dry until grass grew from him up to his head. He did not drink water except that it was mixed with tears, two-thirds of it being tears. He exerted himself, longing for God Most High to pardon him, until he nearly perished. He was occupied with this to the neglect of his kingdom, until a son of his called Iya (Īshā) rose up against his rule and called people to himself, and the people of deviation among the Children of Israel gathered around him. When he (David) was forgiven, he fought against him and defeated him.

﴿And indeed, for him with Us is a nearness (zulfā) and a good place of return﴾, that is, closeness and honour after forgiveness.

﴿and a good place of return﴾, that is, a good place of return in Paradise.

﴿يا داوُدُ إنّا جَعَلْناكَ خَلِيفَةً في الأرْضِ﴾ This is either a narration of what was addressed to him, peace be upon him, clarifying his nearness to Him, glorified and exalted; or it is the object of an implied verb of speech, which is coordinated with *ghafarna* (We forgave), or a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from its agent, meaning: "and We said to him," or "saying to him, O Dawud..." etc. That is, We made you a vicegerent (*istakhlafnaka*) over the kingdom in it and the judgment among its people, or We made you a vicegerent of those prophets before you who upheld the truth. In this there is clear evidence that his state, peace be upon him, after repentance remained exactly as it was before, never having changed at all.

﴿فاحْكم بَيْنَ النّاسِ بِالحَقِّ﴾ by the judgment of God, exalted, for vicegerency in both its senses necessarily requires this.

﴿وَلا تَتَّبِعِ الهَوى﴾ that is, the desire of the soul in judgments and in other matters of religion and worldly affairs.

﴿فَيُضِلَّكَ عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ It is in the subjunctive (*nasb*) as a response to the prohibition (*jawab al-nahy*, the verb following a prohibition that is put in the subjunctive as its consequence). It was also said that it is in the jussive (*majzum*) by coordination with the prohibition, with a fatha because of the meeting of two consonants (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*). That is: the desire, or following it, will be the cause of your straying from its proofs which He set up upon the truth, both in creation and in legislation. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ يَضِلُّونَ عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("Indeed those who stray from the way of God...") is a reason for what precedes it, by explaining its harmful consequence, and the mention of "the way of God" in the place where a pronoun would be expected serves to increase the affirmation and to signal the complete abhorrence of straying from it.

﴿لَهم عَذابٌ شَدِيدٌ﴾ ("For them is a severe punishment.") This is a clause made of a predicate and subject, which occurs as the predicate of *inna* (indeed). Or the prepositional phrase (*al-zarf*) is the predicate of *inna*. The word *'adhab* (punishment) is in the nominative (*marfu'*) as the agent (*fa'iliyya*) of what is implied in it of the meaning of "being established" (*al-istiqrar*).

﴿بِما نَسُوا﴾ ("because they forgot") means: because of their forgetting. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿يَوْمَ الحِسابِ﴾ ("the Day of Reckoning"), it may be the object of *nasu* (they forgot), in which case it is an explicit reason for the establishment of the severe punishment for them, namely their forgetting of the Day of Reckoning, after a hint at the causal relation of what it entails and necessitates, namely straying from the way of God, exalted is He. For straying necessarily entails forgetting the Day of Reckoning altogether; indeed this is one instance of it. Or it may be an adverbial complement (*zarf*) of His saying, exalted is He, "for them" (*lahum*), meaning: for them there is a severe punishment on the Day of Resurrection because of their forgetting, which is an expression for their straying. It necessarily follows that its object is "the way of God," so the explicitly stated reason is then identical with the reason hinted at, though different in form. Whoever does not notice this subtle secret has said: "because of their forgetting," which is their straying from the way, for remembering it requires adhering to the truth and opposing the desire. So reflect.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 27:**

﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain.﴾ This is a resumed sentence (*kalam mustanaf*, a new sentence that begins a fresh clause) that confirms what precedes it concerning the matter of resurrection (*ba'th*), reckoning (*hisab*) and recompense (*jaza'*). That is: We did not create them, nor the created things between them, in this wondrous order which minds are bewildered in understanding, as a creation in vain (*batilan*), meaning empty of a noble purpose and a dazzling wisdom. Rather, it contains a clear truth and far-reaching wisdoms, in that from among what We created We created souls (*nufusan*) in which We placed reason and the ability to distinguish between truth and falsehood and between what benefits and what harms. We enabled them to act, both in knowledge and in practice, to gain their benefits and repel their harms. We set up for the truth signs (*dala'il*) in the horizons and in the souls, and We gave them the capacity to bear witness by them. Then We did not limit Ourselves to this measure of kindnesses (*al-alatif*, divine grace, sing. *lutf*), but We sent to them messengers and sent down to them a clear Book in which is every subtle and great matter, and We removed their impediments (*'ilal*) entirely, and We presented them with obligation (*taklif*) for great benefits, and We prepared for them an outcome and a recompense according to their deeds.

﴿That﴾ refers to what was denied, namely that those things were created in vain.

﴿is the assumption of those who disbelieved﴾: that is, what they assume. Their denial of the matter of resurrection and recompense, upon which the orbit of the formation of the world turns, is a statement from them that the creation of what has been mentioned is in vain and devoid of wisdom. Glorified is He, exalted far above what they say.

﴿So woe to those who disbelieved﴾ is a subject and predicate (*mubtada' wa khabar*). The *fa'* (so) indicates that the establishment of woe (*wayl*) for them follows from their false assumption. Likewise, placing the relative pronoun (*al-ladhina*) in the position of their pronoun indicates, by what lies within the relative clause, that their disbelief is the cause of it, and there is no contradiction between the two, because their assumption is one of the forms of their disbelief. The *min* in His saying ﴿from the Fire﴾ is causal (*ta'lili*), as in His saying ﴿So woe to them for what their hands have written﴾ and its like. It indicates that the Fire is the cause for the explicit establishment of woe for them, after the hint of the causation of what leads to it from their assumption and disbelief. That is: woe to them because of the Fire that results from their assumption and disbelief.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 28:

﴿Shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters on earth?﴾ "Am" (أمْ) is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and what it contains of "bal" (بَلْ) is for a transitional turning away (al-idrab al-intiqali) (idrab: a shift or change of topic, marked by bal) from establishing the matter of the Resurrection, the Reckoning and the Recompense, by what has passed of negating that the world was created devoid of wisdoms and benefits, to establishing and affirming it through what the hamzah (الهَمْزَة) contains of denial of equality between the two groups, and the negation of that in the most eloquent and emphatic manner. That is: "Rather, shall We make the believing, righteous ones like the disbelieving, corrupt ones throughout the lands of the earth?" As would be required by the absence of resurrection and what follows from it of recompense, given the equality of the two groups in enjoying the worldly life. Rather, the disbelievers have a larger share of it than the believers. But that making is impossible. Therefore the Resurrection and the Recompense are necessarily established, to raise the first group to the highest of the highest (a'la 'Illiyyin) and to return the others to the lowest of the low (asfal safilin). And His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Or shall We make the God-fearing like the wicked?﴾ is a turning away (idrab) and a transition from establishing what was mentioned through the implication of an impossibility, which is the equality between the two mentioned groups in general, to establishing it through the implication of something more evidently impossible, which is the equality between the pious believers and the wretched disbelievers. Taking "the wicked" (al-fujjar) to mean the sinful among the believers does not suit the context. It is permissible that these two groups refer to the same first two groups, with the repetition being based on two other attributes which are more emphatic in denying equality than the first two attributes. It is said: the disbelievers of Quraysh said to the believers, "We will be given good in the Hereafter as you will be given." So this verse was revealed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 29:

﴿A Book﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, which is an expression for the Qur'an, or for the surah. His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿We have sent it down to you﴾ is its description. (p-225) His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿blessed﴾ is a second predicate of the subject, or a description of "a Book" according to those who permit placing the explicit description after the non-explicit one. It has also been read as "mubarakan" (مُبارَكًا), as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the object of "anzalna" (we sent down). The meaning of "mubarak" (blessed) is one abundant in religious and worldly benefits. His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿that they may ponder its verses﴾ is connected to "anzalnahu" (We sent it down), meaning: We sent it down so that they would reflect upon its verses, among which are these verses that express the secrets of creation and legislation, so that they would know what its apparent meanings contain of exceptional meanings and fitting interpretations. It has also been read as "liyadabbaru" (لِيَتَدَبَّرُوا) according to the original form, and as "litaddabbaru" (لِتَدَّبَّرُوا) in the second person, meaning: you and the scholars of your community, with one of the two tā' (ت) omitted.

﴿And that those of understanding may take heed﴾, meaning: and that those possessing sound intellects may be admonished by it, or that they may call to mind what is, as it were, fixed in their intellects, owing to their great firmness in knowing it through the proofs established for it, for the divine books clarify what cannot be known except through revelation, and guide to what the intellect has no path to reach.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 30:

﴿And We bestowed upon Dawud Sulayman; how excellent a servant﴾. It is also read (نِعْمَ العَبْدُ) [with the noun in the nominative as a predicate of an implied subject], meaning Sulayman, as is indicated by his being mentioned after Dawud even though he is the direct object of "wahabna" (We bestowed). And [it is indicated] because the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, he was ever oft-returning﴾, i.e., returning to Allah the Exalted in repentance, or returning to glorification (al-tasbih) [of Allah], is a reason (ta'lil) for the praise, and it is from his state, because the pronoun in the genitive in the saying of the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 31:

﴿When it was displayed before him﴾ refers, definitely, back to him (peace and blessings be upon him), and "idh" (when) is in the accusative, governed by "udhkur" (remember), i.e., remember what proceeded from him when it was displayed before him.

﴿In the evening﴾ is from midday until the end of the day.

﴿The swift-footed steeds﴾ for indeed it bears witness that he was oft-returning (awwab). It has been said that it is an adverbial complement of "awwab", and it has been said that it is of "ni'ma" (how excellent). The postponement of "al-safinat" (the swift-footed steeds) behind the two adverbial phrases is due to what has passed many times, namely the building of suspense toward the delayed element. Al-saffin (the one standing on three legs, with one hoof raised) among horses is one that stands on the tip of the hoof of a forefoot or hind foot. It is among the praiseworthy qualities in horses, and it is hardly ever ascribed except to purebred, pure-bred Arab horses. It has also been said that it is the one that gathers its two forelegs and sets them together; as for the one that stands on its hoof with the leg fully down, it is "al-mikhim" (one that stands with the hoof placed firmly).

﴿The fine coursers (al-jiyad)﴾ is the plural of "jawad" and "judud", meaning one that is swift in its running. It has been said that it is one that is generous (yajud) when galloping. It has been said that it was described with stillness and fine quality to explain that it combined the two praiseworthy attributes, standing still and running: when it stood still it was quiet and calm in its positions, and when it ran it was swift and light in its running. It has also been said that it is the plural of "jayyid" (fine). It is narrated that he (peace be upon him) raided the people of Damascus and Nisibis and acquired a thousand horses. It has been said that his father had acquired them from the Amalekites and he inherited them from him. It has been said that they came out of the sea with wings. One day, after he had prayed the midday prayer, he sat on his throne and reviewed them, and they continued to be displayed before him until the sun set, and he neglected the afternoon prayer, or a portion of remembrance (wird) of God that he had at that time. The people were in awe of him and did not inform him, so he grieved over what he had missed, and so he recalled them and slaughtered them, drawing near to God, the Exalted. A hundred remained, and so whatever horses are among the people are from their offspring. It has been said that when he slaughtered them, God replaced them with something better: it is the wind, which runs by his command.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 32:

﴿Then he said, "Indeed, I have loved the love of good (al-khayr) over the remembrance of my Lord."﴾ He (ﷺ) said this at the time of sunset, acknowledging what had proceeded from him of being preoccupied with them (the horses) to the neglect of the prayer, and regretting it, and as a preparation for what follows of the command to return them and slaughter them (cut their legs). The "consequence" (al-ta'qib) is considered with respect to the final parts of the continuous display (al-'ardh al-mustamirr), not its beginning. (p-226) The emphasis (al-ta'kid) serves to indicate that his acknowledgment and regret came from the depths of the heart, not to establish the content of the report. The original construction of "ahbabtu" (I loved) is that it takes "ala" (upon/on); because it has the meaning of "athartu" (I preferred), but when it is substituted in the place of "anbata" (I turned/inclined), it takes its construction, and "hubba al-khayr" (the love of good) is its object, as if it were said: "I inclined the love of good over the remembrance of my Lord," and he placed it in its place. And "al-khayr" (good) means abundant wealth. What is meant by it are the horses, which preoccupied him (peace be upon him). It is possible that he called them "good" because goodness is attached to them.

He (ﷺ) said: ﴿Goodness is tied to the forelocks of horses until the Day of Resurrection.﴾

It was also read as "anni" (with the particle "anna" and the first person pronoun attached). ﴿Until they were hidden by the veil﴾ is connected to his saying "ahbabtu" (I loved), with respect to the continuation and persistence of the love in accordance with the continuation of the display; that is: "I inclined the love of good over the remembrance of my Lord," and that continued until they were hidden, that is, the sun set, likening its setting in its place of setting to the concealment of what is hidden by its veil. Its pronoun is omitted without mention, the evening (al-'ashiyy) indicating it. It was also said: the pronoun refers to "al-safinat" (the poised horses), that is: until they were hidden by the veil of the night, that is, by its darkness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 33:

﴿Bring them back to me.﴾ This is part of the speech of Sulayman (peace be upon him), and it is the target of his aim in putting forward what he put forward. Whoever does not notice this, despite its being apparent, imagines that it is connected to an implied element, serving as the answer to another implied element, as if a questioner had said: "So what did Sulayman (peace be upon him) say?" and it was answered: "He said: Bring them back." So reflect.

The "fa'" (fa) in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so he began to pass his hand over [them], over the shanks and the necks﴾ is an eloquent fa' (fa' al-fasiha), revealing a sentence that has been omitted, relying on the situation as an indication of it and to signal the extreme speed of compliance with the command. That is: so they brought them back to him, and he began to pass over the sword, passing over [it].

﴿Over the shanks and the necks﴾: that is, he cut off their shanks and necks, from the expression of them: "he wiped his neck (masaha 'ilawatahu)," meaning he struck his neck. It was also said: he began to pass his hand over their necks and shanks out of love for them and admiration of them, but this is not the case. It was read "bi-al-su'uq" with the hamza placed on the waw because of its damma, as in "adw'ur" (plural of dar). It was read "bi-al-su'uuq," treating the damma of the sin as if it were the damma of the waw. It was also read "bi-al-saq" (singular), dispensing with the plural because there is no risk of confusion.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 34:

﴿We certainly tested Solomon and placed upon his throne a body, then he turned back in repentance.﴾ The most apparent of what has been said about his trial, peace be upon him, is what has been transmitted in a report traced back to the Prophet (marfu'), that he said: "Tonight I will go round to seventy women, and each one will bear a horseman who will fight in the way of Allah, the Exalted," and he did not say "if Allah wills." So he went round to them, but only one woman conceived, and she bore half a man. By Him in whose hand my soul is, had he said "if Allah wills," they would all have fought in the way of Allah as horsemen.

It was also said: a son was born to him, and the devils gathered to kill him. He learned of this, so he used to nourish the child in the clouds. He was unaware of it until the child was cast onto his throne dead, and so he became aware of his error in not placing his trust in Allah, Mighty and Exalted.

It was also said: he raided Sidon from the islands, killed its king, and captured a daughter of his called Jarada, one of the most beautiful of people. He chose her for himself, and she made him love her. She could not stop her tears out of grief for her father. So he ordered the devils, and they fashioned an image of him for her. She would go out to it and return, along with her maidservants, and they would prostrate to her as they had been accustomed to do in his kingdom. Asif informed him of this, so he broke the image, punished the woman, then went out alone to a barren land. Ashes were spread for him, and he sat upon them, repenting to Allah, the Exalted, weeping and humbling himself.

He had a umm walad (a slave woman who had borne him a child) called Amina. Whenever he entered for purification or to approach a woman, he would give her his ring, and his kingship was in it. One day he gave it to her, and a devil called Sakhr took on the form of his likeness, took the ring and put it on, and sat upon his throne. The people gathered around him and his command was carried out in everything except with his wives. Solomon had changed in appearance, so he came to Amina to ask for the ring, but she denied him and drove him away. Then he knew that the sin had overtaken him, so he went around the houses begging for food. Whenever he said, "I am Solomon," they threw dust on him and cursed him. Then he went to the fishermen and carried fish for them, and they gave him two fish each day. He remained in this state for forty mornings, corresponding to the number of days the idol had been worshipped in his house. Asif and the leaders of the Children of Israel then denounced the rule of the devil. Then the accursed one flew away and threw the ring into the sea. A fish swallowed it and fell into the hand of Solomon, who split open its belly and found the ring in it. He put it on, fell down in prostration, and his kingship returned to him. He hollowed out a rock for Sakhr, placed him inside, closed it with another rock, bound them both with iron and lead, and cast him into the sea.

According to this view, "body" refers to a rock that was named after him, and it is a body without a soul, because it took on a form that was not as it was. The sin was his negligence, peace be upon him, regarding the state of his household, since making images was not forbidden at that time. And the prostration of the image without his knowledge does not harm him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 35:

﴿He said﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "anaba" (turned in repentance), and an explanation (tafsir) of it.

﴿My Lord, forgive me﴾ i.e., the slip that proceeded from me.

﴿And grant me a kingdom such as shall not belong to anyone after me﴾: that it not be made easy for anyone else, and that it not be (a kingdom) that would be a miracle (mu'jizah) for me suited to my circumstances. For indeed he, upon him be blessings and peace, when he grew up in the house of kingship and prophethood and inherited both together, requested from his Lord a miracle comprehensive of the ruling of both. Or (it means): "No one should be permitted to strip it from me after this stripping." Or: "It is not proper for anyone after me, because of its greatness," like your saying about so-and-so: "There is none like him in virtue and wealth," intending to describe the kingdom as great, not that no one else be given the like of it, which would be rivalry (munafasah). It was also said: it was a great kingdom, and he feared that someone else might be given the like of it, and then would not safeguard the limits of God, exalted is He. Placing the seeking of forgiveness before the seeking of a gift is for greater concern for the matter of religion, following the practice (sunan) of the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, and the righteous, and because that is more conducive to acceptance. It was also recited as "li" (لِيَ) with the ya' vowelled with a fatha.

﴿Indeed You, You are the Bestower﴾ is a reason (ta'lil) for the supplication for forgiveness and gift together, not for the last alone, for forgiveness too is certainly among the attributes of the quality of bestowing (al-wahhabiyyah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 36:

﴿So We subjected the wind to him﴾ means: We made it submissive to his command, in response to his supplication. Thus his affairs, peace be upon him, returned to what they had been before the trial (fitnah). It is also read: (al-riyāḥa, the plural "winds"). ﴿Running at his command﴾ explains its subjection to him. ﴿Gently﴾ means soft and pleasant, from softness, not violently shaking. It was also said: obedient, not resisting him, like a commanded subordinate who submits.

﴿Wherever he intended﴾ means wherever he aimed and wished. Al-Asma'i related from the Arabs: "He hit the correct thing (aṣāba al-ṣawāb) but missed the answer (fa-akhṭa'a al-jawāb)."

"And the devils" is a conjunction (ʿatf) coordinated with "the wind."

"Every builder and diver" is a substitution (badal) from "the devils."

﴿And [others] bound together in fetters.﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on "every builder," and it falls under the same ruling as the substitution (badal). It is as if, peace be upon him, he had divided the devils into workers, whom he employed in arduous tasks such as building, diving, and the like, and into rebels, some of whom were bound together with one another in chains so as to restrain them from evil and corruption. Perhaps their bodies are translucent, so they are not seen, and they are solid, so they can be shackled, and they are able to perform difficult labors. It has also been permitted that the binding in fetters be an expression for restraining them from evils by way of figurative representation. The ṣafd (fetter) is a shackle, and the word is also used for a gift, because it binds the one who receives it to the benefactor. They distinguished between the two verbs: ṣafadahu means "he shackled him," while aṣfadahu means "he gave him," the reverse of waʿada and awʿadahu (to promise and to threaten). And the words of the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 39:

﴿This﴾ . . . etc. It is either a narration of what was addressed to Solomon, peace be upon him, showing the greatness of the dominion he was given and that it was entrusted to him in a complete delegation; or it is an implied speech (maqul muqaddar) coordinated with "We subjected" (sakhkharna), or a circumstantial clause (hal) from its agent, as was mentioned at the conclusion of the story of David, peace be upon him. That is: and We said to him, or saying to him: "This matter which We have given you of great dominion, and expansiveness, and authority over what no one other than you has been given authority over."

﴿Our gift﴾ specific to you.

﴿So bestow or withhold﴾: give to whom you wish, and withhold from whom you wish.

﴿Without account﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun hidden in the imperative (al-mustakinn fi al-amr), meaning: not being held to account for anything of it; and withholding it is the delegation of disposal over it to you without restriction. Or it is a circumstantial clause from the gift (al-ata'), meaning: this is Our gift, combined with being without account, because of its great abundance. Or it is a complement (silah) to it, and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) according to both interpretations. It has also been said: the reference is to the subjugation of the devils. The intended meaning of bestowing (mann) and withholding (imsak) is: granting liberty and restriction.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 40:

﴿And indeed, for him with Us is a near station (zulfa)﴾ in the Hereafter, along with the great kingdom he had in this world.

﴿And a good final return﴾ is Paradise. It is said: Sulayman (peace be upon him) was tried after he had ruled for twenty years, and he ruled for twenty years after the trial. The jurist Abu Hanifa Ahmad ibn Dawud al-Dinawari (d. c. 282 AH) mentioned in his History that Sulayman (peace be upon him) inherited his father's kingdom in the era of Kaykhusraw ibn Siyavash, and travelled from Syria to Iraq. News of him reached Kaykhusraw, so he fled to Khurasan, and he did not remain long before he died. Then Sulayman (peace be upon him) travelled to Marw, then to the lands of the Turks, and penetrated deep into them. Then he crossed the lands of China, then turned back until he reached the land of Persia, and stayed there for some days. Then he returned to Syria, and then ordered the building of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). When he had finished it, he travelled to Tihama, then to San'a, and of his story with its queen was what Allah the Exalted mentioned. He also campaigned in the lands of the Maghrib, Andalusia, Tangier and others. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 41:

﴿And mention Our servant Ayyub﴾: it is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "mention Our servant Dawud." The story of Sulayman is not introduced with this heading because of the complete connection between him and Dawud, peace be upon them both. Ayyub is the son of ʿIs ibn Ishaq, peace be upon him.

﴿When he called out to his Lord﴾: a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from "Our servant," and "Ayyub" is an explanatory appositive (ʿatf bayan) to it.

﴿That﴾: meaning "that" (anni), ﴿the Shaytan has touched me﴾, with the ya' of "massani" vocalised with a fatha. It has also been read with it being sukun and with it being dropped.

﴿with hardship﴾: that is, with fatigue (nasb). It has been read with a fatha on the nun, with two fathas, and with two dammas for emphasis (li-l-tathqil).

﴿and affliction﴾: that is, pain and ailment (wasab), meaning his illness and what he suffered of the various kinds of hardships. This is what is meant by the "harm" in His words: ﴿that harm has touched me﴾. It is a quotation of his words with the wording he used when he called out, for otherwise it would have been said that "it touched him..." and so on. The attribution to the Shaytan is either because God touched him with that on account of what he did through his whispering, as it is said that he was made to admire the abundance of his wealth; or because a wronged man sought his help and he did not help him; or because his livestock were in the territory of a disbelieving king and he flattered him and did not fight him; or to test his patience, in which case it is an acknowledgment of the sin; or (p-229) out of observance of etiquette; or because he whispered to his followers until they rejected him and expelled him from their homes; or because the intended meaning of "hardship" is what the Shaytan used to whisper to him during his illness, magnifying the calamity that had befallen him, despairing of mercy, and urging him toward aversion and impatience. So he turned to God Most High that He might suffice him in that by removing the affliction, or by granting him success in repelling and warding it off through patient endurance. This is not the complete form of his supplication, peace be upon him; rather, among its parts is his saying: ﴿and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾. He therefore dispensed here with mentioning it, relying on what is in Surah al-Anbiya', just as he omitted there the mention of the Shaytan, relying on what is mentioned here. And the saying of God Most High:

﴿Strike with your foot﴾ ... etc. Either it is a narration of what was said to him, or it is a quoted speech introduced by an implied saying coordinated with "nādā" (called out), meaning: So We said to him, "Strike with your foot," i.e., strike the earth with it.
