Likewise His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This is a cool bath and a drink﴾, for it too is either a narration of what was said to him after he complied with the command and the water gushed forth, or a quoted speech introduced by an implied saying coordinated with an implied element that the discourse leads to. As if it were said: So he struck it and a spring gushed forth, so We said to him, "This is a bath you may wash in and drink from, and your outward and inward will be healed." It is also said: two springs gushed forth, one hot for bathing and one cold for drinking. But the apparent sense of the noble text rejects this, as does His saying, Exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 43:

﴿And We gave him his family﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon an implied clause (muqaddar) that is itself consequent upon another implied clause, which the implied speech mentioned just before (al-qawl al-muqaddar anifan) necessitates. It is as if it were said: "So he washed and drank, and thereby We removed the harm that was upon him, as in surah al-Anbiya'." And "We gave him his family" is either by restoring them to life after their death, which is what is related from al-Hasan, or by gathering them after their dispersal, as has been said.

﴿And the like of them with them﴾ is coordinated upon "his family," so he had, of offspring, double what he had before.

﴿As a mercy from Us﴾ meaning: as a great mercy upon him from Our side.

﴿And a reminder for those of understanding﴾ and so that they may be reminded of this, in order that they endure hardships as he endured, and turn to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in what befalls them, just as he turned to Him, so that He might deal with them as He dealt with him, with a good end.

﴿وَخُذْ بِيَدِكَ ضِغْثًا﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) either with "ارْكُضْ" (ірком: "irkud", "strike the ground with your foot") or with "وَهَبْنا" ("We gave"), by supposing an implied "قُلْنا" (We said), so that the sense is: "and We said, 'Take in your hand...'" ... etc. The first is closer in wording, but this is more fitting in meaning, for the need for this command does not arise except after recovery of health. His wife was Rahmah bint Ifraim ibn Yusuf. It is also said: Liya bint Ya'qub, and it is said: Masir bint Misha ibn Yusuf (peace be upon him). She went out on an errand and was late, so he swore that if he recovered he would strike her one hundred blows. So God Most High commanded him to take the dhigth. The dhigth (a bundle of grass) is a small bundle of grass or the like. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): "a handful of twigs." And He said: ﴿فاضْرِبْ بِهِ﴾ ("then strike with it"), i.e., with that dhigth.

﴿وَلا تَحْنَثْ﴾ ("and do not break your oath"), in your oath, for piety (al-birr) is realized by it. God, glorified is He, prescribed this concession (rukhsa) as mercy upon him and upon her, because of her good service to him and his pleasure with her, and it remains in effect. It is required that each of the hundred strokes reach the one struck, either with the ends of the bundle upright, or with its sides laid flat in the form of striking.

﴿إنّا وجَدْناهُ صابِرًا﴾ ("Indeed, We found him patient") in what befell him concerning himself, his family and his property. His complaint to God Most High does not detract from this, for it is not called impatience (jaza'), just as wishing for well-being and seeking healing is not. Moreover, he said that out of fear of temptation in religion, since Satan was whispering to his people that if he were a prophet he would not have been tried with what he was tried with. And the desire for the strength to obey—his condition had reached the point where nothing remained of him except the heart and the tongue. It is related that he (peace be upon him) said in his private supplication (munajat): "My God, You know that my tongue never contradicted my heart, my heart never followed my eye, I never gave what my right hand possessed, I never ate while an orphan was with me, and I never spent the night sated or clothed while a hungry or naked person was with me." Then God Most High removed his affliction from him.

﴿نِعْمَ العَبْدُ﴾ ("How excellent a servant"), i.e., Ayyub.

﴿إنَّهُ أوّابٌ﴾ ("Indeed he was one who turns back often") is an explanation for his praise, i.e., one who constantly returns to God Most High.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 45:

﴿And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac and Jacob﴾ — an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to "Our servants." It is also read as "ʿabdanā" (His servant). Either Abraham alone is in apposition, for the sake of his greater honour, while the other two are joined to "ʿabdanā" by conjunction; or it is said to be a substitution (badal), or it is put in the accusative by an implied "aʿnī" (I mean). Or, "ʿabdanā" is a generic noun (ism jins) placed in the position of the plural.

﴿Possessors of strength and vision﴾ — possessors of strength in obedience and insight in religion; or possessors of noble deeds and lofty knowledge. He used "hands" to denote deeds, because most deeds are carried out by them, and "eyes" to denote knowledge, because sight is the strongest of its sources. In this there is an allusion (taʿrīḍ) to the ignorant idlers that they are like the disabled and the blind, and a rebuke for their abandoning striving (mujāhada) and reflection (taʾammul) while they are able to do both. It is also read as "ʾulī al-ayd" with the yāʾ dropped and the kasra kept as sufficient, and as "ʾulī al-ayādī" according to the plural of the plural.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 46:

﴿Indeed, We made them pure with a pure quality﴾ is an explanation (ta'lil) of what they were described with, of the nobility of servitude (ubudiyyah) and the elevated rank in knowledge and action. That is: We made them sincerely devoted to Us by means of a pure quality of great significance, as the indefinite form used for magnification (al-tankir al-tafkhimi) indicates. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the remembrance of the Abode﴾ is an clarification of the "pure quality" after its vagueness, for the sake of magnification. That is: a constant remembrance of the Hereafter, for their sincerity in obedience is due to their remembrance of it. This is because the aim of their gaze and the target of their thoughts, in all that they do and refrain from, is the neighborhood of Allah, mighty and majestic, and the attainment of meeting Him, and that is only possible in the Hereafter. It was also said: We made them pure by granting them success in it (tawfiq) and by showing kindness to them in choosing it (lutf). The first view is supported by the reading of those who read (bi-khalisatihim) ["by their pure [quality]"], and by the unqualified use of "the Abode," which signals that it is the true abode, while this world is merely a passageway. It was also read with "pure" (khalisah) being in construct with "remembrance" (dhikra), meaning: by what is purely from the remembrance of the Abode, in the sense that they do not mix its remembrance with anything else at all; or, their reminding [others of] the Hereafter, their encouraging [people] toward it, and their discouraging [them] from this world, as is the practice of the Prophets, peace be upon them. It was also said: "the remembrance of the Abode" is a good reputation in this world, and a tongue of truthfulness that belongs to no one else.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And indeed they are with Us among the chosen, the best.﴾

Those chosen from among their peers, selected for goodness over them. "Al-akhyar" is the plural of khayr, like sharr and ashrar. It is also said that it is the plural of khayyir, or of a form lightened from it, like amwat as the plural of mayyit and mayt.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 48:

﴿And mention Ismail.﴾ His mention is singled out from that of his father and his brother, to indicate his eminence in patience, which is the purpose of the reminder.

﴿And al-Yasa'.﴾ He is the son of Akhtub, son of al-'Ajuz. Ilyas (Elijah) appointed him as successor over the Children of Israel, and then he was made a prophet. The "al-" in it (al-Yasa') is the definite article (harf al-ta'rif) that entered upon Yasa', as in the saying of one who said: "I saw al-Walid ibn al-Yazid blessed." It was also read: ﴿wa-al-Yasa'u﴾. It is as if its original form was Layasa', a pattern of fay'al derived from al-lash' (the sting), to which the definite article was attached. It has also been said that, according to both readings, it is a non-Arabic proper name to which the "al-" was attached. It has also been said that it is Yusha' (Joshua).

﴿And Dhu al-Kifl.﴾ He is the cousin of Yasa', or Bishr ibn Ayyub. Scholars differed about his prophethood and his epithet. It has been said that one hundred prophets of the Children of Israel fled to him from killing, and he sheltered them and took responsibility for them (kafala-hum). It has also been said that he took responsibility for the deeds of a righteous man who used to pray one hundred prayers every day.

﴿And all of them﴾ means: all of them.

﴿are among the best (al-akhyar)﴾: those well known for goodness.

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 49:

﴿This﴾ is a reference to what preceded of the verses that speak of their virtues.

﴿a reminder﴾ i.e., an honour for them, and a good mention by which they will be remembered forever. Or it is a kind of the remembrance, which is the Qur'an, and a section of it that includes the reports of the Prophets, peace be upon them. And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "This is the mention of those Prophets who passed away."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, for the righteous there is a good place of return﴾ is the beginning of an explanation of their abundant reward in the Hereafter, after the explanation of their good mention in this world. This is another section of the sections of the Revelation. By "the righteous" (al-muttaqin) is meant either the category in general, and they enter the ruling primarily, or the very ones previously mentioned, described by this term to praise them for taqwa (God-consciousness), which is the farthest end of perfection.

Gardens of Eden (jannāt ʿAdn) are an appositive (ʿaṭf bayān) to ḥusn maʾāb according to those who permit their differing in definiteness and indefiniteness, since ʿAdn is definite by virtue of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Gardens of Eden, which the Most Merciful has promised to His servants﴾. Or it is a substitute (badal) from it, or it is in the accusative on the basis of praise (naṣb ʿalā al-madḥ).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their doors are opened for them﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from jannāt ʿAdn. The governing element (al-ʿāmil) in it is the sense of the verb contained in lil-muttaqīn (for the God-conscious). The word al-abwāb (the doors) is in the nominative as a passive participle (ism al-mafʿūl). The linking element (al-rābiṭ) between the circumstantial clause and its referent is either a implied pronoun, as is the view of the Basrans, meaning: "the doors of them" (al-abwāb minhā); or it is the definite article alif-lam standing in place of the pronoun, as is the view of the Kufans, since the original is abwābuhā (its doors).

Both words may be read in the nominative, as a subject and predicate (mubtadaʾ wa-khabar), or as two predicates of an elided subject, meaning: "They are the Gardens of Eden; they are opened (for them)."

Here's the translation:

﴿Reclining therein﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to the pronoun in ﴿for them﴾, and the element governing it (al-ʿāmil fīhā) is "mufattaḥatan" (opened). The Exalted's statement ﴿calling therein for abundant fruit and drink﴾ is a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf) explaining their condition therein. It has also been said that it too is a circumstantial clause relating to what was mentioned, or to the pronoun in "reclining." Limiting the mention to calling for fruit serves to indicate that their food is purely for enjoyment and delight, not for nourishment, since nourishment is for replacing what is dissipated (badal al-mutaḥallil), and nothing there is dissipated.

**﴿And with them are those who restrain their glances﴾**, meaning they are devoted to their husbands and do not look at anyone else.

**﴿Atrāb﴾** (أتراب) means peers of the same age as them, since affection between equals is firmer. Or it means that they are of an age with one another, with none of them being an old woman or a young girl. Its derivation (*ishtiqāq*) is from *turāb* (dust), because they all touch [the dust] at the same time.

This is the commentary on Qur'an 38:53, with the verse rendered as it stands. Translating the passage:

﴿This is what you are promised, for the Day of Reckoning.﴾ That is: for its sake. For the reckoning is the cause (ʿillah) of arriving at the recompense. It has also been read with the yāʾ (as yuwāfiq, "to agree with") so that it accords with what precedes it. (p-232) The shift in address (iltifāt, a change from one grammatical person to another) is more fitting to the context of favour and honour.

Indeed, this (i.e., what has been mentioned of the varieties of blessings and noble gifts).

﴿Indeed, it is Our provision﴾, which We have given you, ﴿that has no end﴾, no cessation ever.

﴿This﴾, i.e., the matter is this, or this is as has been mentioned, or this is a reminder. His words, exalted is He, ﴿And indeed for the transgressors is an evil place of return﴾, begin the explanation of the opposites of the preceding group.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 56:

﴿Jahannam﴾ its i'rab (grammatical analysis) is as has preceded.

﴿yaslawnaha﴾ i.e., they enter it; it is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to Jahannam.

﴿fa-bi'sa al-mihad﴾ "al-mihad" is the bed and the spread, used figuratively from the bedding of a sleeper. The thing particularized by the dispraise is omitted, and it is Jahannam, owing to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For them there is a bed of Jahannam﴾.

﴿This, so let them taste it.﴾ Meaning: let them taste this. So let them taste it, and it is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and fear Me, and Me alone﴾ [2:40]. Or, the punishment is this, so let them taste it. Or, "this" is a *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence), whose *khabar* (predicate) is ﴿boiling water and dark, dank pus﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause (*i'tiraḍ*). According to the first two readings, it is the *khabar* of an omitted *mubtada'*, meaning: it is boiling water. *Ghassaq* is what drips (*yaghsiq*) from the pus of the people of the Fire, from *ghasaqat al-'ayn*, when its tears flowed. It was also said: the boiling water burns with its heat, and the *ghassaq* burns with its cold. It was also said: if one drop of it dripped in the east, it would stink the people of the west, and if one drop dripped in the west, it would stink the people of the east. It was also said: the *ghassaq* is a punishment that none knows except Allah, exalted is He. It was also recited with the *sin* lightened (*takhfif al-sin*).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 58:

﴿And other punishments of similar kind﴾ i.e., another taste (madhuq) or another punishment of the like of this taste, or of the punishment, in its severity and dreadfulness. It is also read: (wa-ukharu), i.e., and other tastes, or other kinds of punishment; and the singularity of the pronoun in "shaklihi" is by interpreting it as referring to what has been mentioned, or to the drink (sharab) which encompasses the hamim (boiling water) and the ghassaq (intensely cold, fetid liquid), or it refers back to the ghassaq.

﴿azwaj﴾ i.e., kinds (ajnas). It is the predicate (khabar) of "akhar", since it is permissible for it to be "durub" (sorts), or an attributive adjective (sifa) of it, or of the three (things), or it is in the nominative case by virtue of the preposition-phrase, with the predicate omitted, like "lahum" (for them).

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 59:

﴿This is a host rushing in with you.﴾ It is a report of what is said by the guardians (al-khazanah) of the Fire to the leaders of the tyrants when they enter the Fire, and a host that used to follow them in disbelief and misguidance rushes in with them. Al-iqtiham (rushing in) is entering something with force. Al-Raghib said: al-iqtiham is plunging into the midst of a frightening hardship. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No welcome for them!﴾ is part of the completion of the guardians' speech, by way of invocation against the host; or it is a description of the host; or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to them, meaning: it is said, or said concerning them, "No welcome for them!", that is, "They did not come to a welcome," or "The abode has not made them welcome in a spacious manner."

﴿Indeed, they are the ones who will burn in the Fire.﴾ This is a justification from the guardians for the host deserving the invocation against them, or for describing them with what has been mentioned. It has also been said: "No welcome for them" up to here is the speech of the leaders concerning their followers, when the guardians address them about the host rushing in with them, expressing their weariness at being joined with them and their aversion to accompanying them. It has also been said: all of that is the speech of the leaders, some of them with others, concerning the followers.

(p-233)

﴿They say﴾: that is, the followers, upon hearing what was said about them. The way they address the leaders in their words, ﴿Nay, it is you! There is no welcome for you﴾ ... etc. On the last two interpretations it is clear. As for the first interpretation, they may have addressed the leaders directly, although the apparent course would have been to say, by way of apology to the guardians of the Fire, "Nay, there is no welcome for them..." etc. They did so intending to show their sincerity by speaking directly to the leaders, and by appealing to the guardians hoping for their judgment in lessening their punishment or doubling the punishment of their adversaries. That is, "Nay, you are more deserving of what was said to us, or what you said." And His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿You brought it upon us﴾ is a reason for their being more deserving of it, that is: you brought the punishment, or the blazing Fire (al-Sili), upon us, and caused us to fall into it by putting forward what leads to it of false beliefs and evil deeds, adorning them in our eyes, and enticing us toward them, not that we engaged in them on our own initiative.

﴿Wretched is the abode﴾: that is, wretched is the dwelling place, Hell. By condemning it they intended to magnify the offense of the leaders against them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 61:

﴿And they said﴾: that is, the followers also. Their placing it between their two statements is because of the clear contrast between them in essence and address; that is, they said, turning away from their dispute, humbly supplicating to God Most High.

﴿Our Lord, whoever brought this upon us, then increase him in punishment, double, in the Fire﴾, like their saying: ﴿Our Lord, these have led us astray, so give them a double punishment from the Fire﴾. That is, a multiplied punishment, meaning one possessing doubling. This is by adding to it its like, so that it becomes double, as in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, give them double the punishment﴾. Or it was said: the intended meaning of "doubling" is the serpents and the vipers.

["And they said"] That is: the tyrants (al-taghun).

﴿What is [the matter] with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the wicked?﴾ They mean the poor among the Muslims, whom they used to despise and mock.

﴿Did We take them as objects of mockery?﴾ The interrogative hamza (hamzat al-istifham) was dropped, so that the hamza of connection (hamzat al-wasl) takes its place. The sentence is resumptive (isti'naf, a new sentence that begins a fresh statement) and has no place in the grammatical analysis (i'rab). They said this in denial against themselves, rebuking themselves for having mocked them.

﴿Or have our eyes turned away from them?﴾ This is connected (muttasil) to ﴿ittakhadhnahum﴾, with ﴿am﴾ being a connected "am" (am al-muttasila, the "or" that links two alternatives). The meaning is: which of the two things did we do to them, mocking them, or belittling and despising them? And our eyes were turning away from them and overlooking them. This is a denial of each of the two actions made against themselves, as a rebuke to themselves. Or it is disconnected (munqati'a, the "or" that begins a new question), and the meaning is: "We took them as objects of mockery, but rather our eyes turned away from them," like your saying: "Is Zayd with you, or is 'Amr with you?" meaning a rebuke of themselves for mocking. Then there is a transition (idrab) from that to a rebuke for despising and belittling.

It is also read ﴿ittakhadhnahum﴾ without a hamza, on the basis that it is another attributive description (sifah) of ﴿rijalan﴾ (men). Then his saying, exalted is He, ﴿or have our eyes turned away﴾ is connected to his saying ﴿What is the matter with us that we do not see﴾, and the meaning is: "What is the matter with us that we do not see them in the Fire? Are they not in it, and is that why we do not see them? Or have our eyes turned away from them while they are in it?!" It has also been permitted that the hamza be implied (muqaddarah) in this reading.

It is read ﴿sukhriyyan﴾ with a dammah on the sin.

(p-234) ﴿Surely that﴾, i.e., what He has related of their states.

﴿is indeed the truth﴾, which must certainly come to pass without fail. His, exalted be He, statement ﴿the disputing of the people of the Fire﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence serves as an explanation of that. In the initial vagueness followed by the clarification, there is further affirmation of it. It has been said that it is a substitute (badal) for the place (mahall) of ﴿that﴾; it has been said that it is a substitute for ﴿truth﴾, or an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to it. It has also been read in the accusative, on the basis that it is a substitute for ﴿that﴾. As for what has been said, that it is an attributive adjective (sifah) to it, it has been objected: the demonstrative (ism al-ishara) is not described except by a definite noun with the definite article (al-); one says "bi-hadha al-rajul" (with this man), and one does not say "bi-hadha ghulam al-rajul" (with this servant of the man).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 65:

﴿Say﴾: a command to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to say to the polytheists: ﴿Indeed, I am only a warner﴾, sent from His direction, warning you of His punishment.

﴿And there is no god﴾ in existence ﴿except Allah, the One﴾, who does not admit partnership or plurality in any way at all.

﴿The Subduer﴾ over everything other than Him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 66:

﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ of the created beings. How, then, could it be imagined that He has a partner from among them?! ﴿The All-Mighty﴾, who cannot be overcome in any of His affairs.

﴿The Oft-Forgiving﴾, the one who abounds in forgiveness, forgiving whom He wills, to whom He wills. In these attributes there is, beyond what is obvious, the affirmation of tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), the promise to those who affirm His oneness, and the warning to the polytheists; and [there is] the repetition of the two attributes of subjugation and might, which convey a sense of warning, and their being placed before the attribute of forgiveness, in order to give the station of warning its due right.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 67:

﴿Say﴾: The repetition of the command ("say") serves to notify that what is to be said is a matter of great importance and grave consequence, which must be attended to, both in acting upon it and in complying with it.

﴿He﴾: i.e., what I have informed you of, namely that I am a warner from His side, that He, exalted is He, is One with no partner, and that He is characterized by the sublime attributes that have been mentioned. The more apparent view is that "He" refers to the Qur'an, and what has been mentioned is included in it by primary inclusion, as the end of the noble surah bears witness. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada.

﴿a great news﴾ that comes from Him, exalted is He. And His exalted saying:

﴿You are turning away from it.﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnaf, a new sentence that begins a fresh point) censuring them for their evil conduct toward it, by showing that they do not appreciate its sublime worth, in that they turn away from it despite its greatness and its being something that calls for wholehearted attention to it and for receiving it with good acceptance. It is also said that it is another attributive description (ṣifah) of "naba'" (tidings). And the words of Allah the Exalted:

﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly﴾ . . . etc. This is a resumptive clause (istinaf) brought to establish that it is a great report, sent from Him, exalted is He, by mentioning one of His reports in detail without any prior knowledge of it on his part and without having taken any of its usual causes. This is a clear proof that it comes by way of revelation (wahy) from Allah, exalted is He, and that all His prophets are likewise. The Exalted Assembly (al-Mala' al-A'la) are the angels, Adam, peace be upon them, and Iblis, may the curse of Allah be upon him. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿when they were disputing﴾ is connected to an omitted element required by the context, since the intended meaning is the negation of his, peace and blessings be upon him, knowledge of their condition (p-235) and not of their essences. The sense is: "I had no knowledge at all, in any respect, of the condition of the Exalted Assembly at the time of their dispute." The wording of the sentence as preferred by the majority of scholars (al-Jumhur) restricts what is broad, for his, peace and blessings be upon him, knowledge is not confined to the statements exchanged among them alone but encompasses them, as well as the actions, such as the prostration of the angels and the arrogance and disbelief of Iblis, as conveyed by revelation. Therefore the negation must necessarily be understood as general as well. His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 70:

﴿Say: It is only revealed to me that I am a plain warner.﴾ This is a parenthetical statement placed between the general mention of their dispute and its detailed account, serving to affirm the reality of the Messenger's knowledge (peace and blessings be upon him) and to specify its cause. However, since the statement of its absence in what preceded, when it indicates its presence now, and since it is clear that he (peace and blessings be upon him) was not connected to any of its familiar sources, it is determined that it is none other than by way of revelation, necessarily. Thus this is made a matter of established certainty, needing no deliberate informing about it, and the purpose and the object of benefit is the informing of what calls to revelation and validates it, in verification of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿I am only a warner﴾, within the verification of his (peace and blessings be upon him) knowledge of the story of the Exalted Assembly. The one standing in place of the subject of "yuha" (is revealed) is either a pronoun referring to the implied state, or what encompasses it and other things. So the meaning is: what is revealed to me concerning the state of the Exalted Assembly, or: what is revealed to me is what is revealed of the unseen matters, of which their state is one, except that I am a plain warner from Him, the Exalted, for his (peace and blessings be upon him) being such is among the motives for revelation to him and among its necessary requirements. As for the one standing in place of the subject being the prepositional phrase, or being "innama ana nadhirun mubin" without assuming the prepositional phrase, and the meaning being: what is revealed to me is only for warning, or: what is revealed to me is only that I warn and convey and do not neglect in that, as has been said. Along with what this involves of the necessity of forced effort in directing the restriction of revelation to its being for warning in the first case, and restricting it to warning in the second, the context and flow of the noble composition do not support it. How could it be otherwise, since the parenthetical statement would then be unrelated to what lies between it and the general and detailed account of the dispute? So reflect, and God is the Guide. It has been read: (innama) with a kasra, on the basis of narration (direct speech). And His, the Exalted's, saying:

﴿When your Lord said to the angels﴾: This begins the detailed explanation of the "disputing" (ikhtisam) mentioned in general terms, which is the exchange of words that took place between them. Since His speaking to them, may He be exalted, was through an angel, it is correct to attribute the disputing to the angels. The clause ﴿idh﴾ (when) is a *badal* (substitution or apposition, a grammatical term meaning a noun that replaces the preceding one) for the first ﴿idh﴾. It is not necessary for the substitution that the word be governed by the same disputing; it is enough that what falls within its scope includes it, since the narrative clearly expresses that in detail. The mention of the title of Lordship (rububiyyah) together with its attachment to his pronoun, upon him be blessings and peace, is to honour him and to indicate that the revelation of this news to him is a nurturing and a support for him, upon him be blessings and peace. The "kaf" (the "your" in "your Lord") is used in view of the state of the one giving the command, because it is more indicative that this is a revelation sent down from Him, may He be exalted, as in His words: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [39:53], etc., and not in view of the state of the one commanded; otherwise it would have said "my Lord," since he is included within the scope of the command.

﴿Indeed I am going to create﴾: that is, in what is to come. In it there is a meaning not present in the form of the present tense: that He, may He be exalted, is definitively the doer of it, without any diverting factor that turns it away, nor any inclination that bends it back.

﴿a human (basharan)﴾: It was said: that is, a dense body that is touched and handled. It was also said: a creature whose skin is bare, without wool or hair. Perhaps what occurred at the time of the event narrated was not this name, since its referent had not yet been created, let alone being named by it; rather it is an expression revealing his condition, and He only expressed it by this name at the time of narration.

﴿from clay (tin)﴾: He did not address its attributes of change, blackening, and being moulded (*masnunah*), being content with what was mentioned in other passages.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 72:

﴿So when I have fashioned him﴾ i.e., I have formed him in the human shape and the human creation, or I have fashioned the parts of his body by balancing his natures (taʿdil tabaʾiʿihi).

﴿And breathed into him of My spirit﴾. The nafkh (blowing) is the passage of wind into the hollow of a body suitable for holding it and being filled with it. There is no actual blowing and no blown-into thing; rather, it is a figurative depiction of the bestowing of that by which life becomes actual upon the matter receptive to it, i.e., when I have perfected its readiness (istiʿdad) and bestowed upon it the spirit by which it lives, which is of My command.

﴿Then fall down to him﴾ is an imperative from waqaʿa (to fall), and in it is evidence that what is commanded is not merely bowing, as has been said. That is: prostrate yourselves to him.

﴿In prostration﴾ as a greeting to him and an honouring of him.

﴿So the angels prostrated﴾ i.e., He created him, shaped him, and breathed into him the spirit, and so the angels prostrated to him.

﴿all of them﴾ such that not one of them remained who did not prostrate.

﴿together﴾ i.e., by way of simultaneity, such that none of them lagged behind any other in it. The meaning of this is not restricted to the state of (ḥāliyya, the circumstantial sense), but it also serves emphasis (ta'kīd). It was said: it was emphasized with two emphatic words for the sake of intensifying the generality. As for whether their prostration here was consequent upon the conditional command that is related, as this noble verse and the one in Surat al-Hijr require, for their apparent meaning calls for its being consequent upon it without anything intervening between them other than what the eloquent fa' (al-fā' al-faṣīḥa, the fa' that indicates an implied intervening stage) makes explicit, namely the creation, the shaping, and the breathing of the spirit; or whether it was upon an immediate command, as what is in Surat al-Baqara, Surat al-A'raf, Surat Bani Isra'il, Surat al-Kahf, and Surat Ta-Ha requires, from the noble verses, its verification has already passed, by the grace of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in Surat al-Baqara and Surat al-A'raf.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 74:

﴿Except Iblis﴾ This is an exception of the connected kind (istithna' muttasil), on the ground that he was a single jinn, hidden among thousands of angels and described with their attributes, so that they overwhelmed him; then he was excepted as one of them (istithna' wahid minhum). Or, because the angels are a kind (jins) that reproduce, and he was one of them. Or it is a disconnected exception (munqati'). His words, exalted is He: ﴿he was arrogant﴾, according to the first view, form a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the manner of his refraining from prostration, which is implied by the exception. For his refraining might be due to deliberation and reflection, and it is with this that it becomes clear that it was out of refusal and arrogance. According to the second view, it may be connected to what precedes it, meaning: "But Iblis was arrogant."

﴿And he was among the disbelievers﴾ That is: he became one of them by his disobedience of the command and his arrogance toward obedience; or he was among them in the knowledge of God, mighty and majestic.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 75:

﴿He said: "O Iblis, what prevented you from prostrating to that which I created with My Two Hands?"﴾ That is: I created him directly, without the intermediary of a father and a mother. The dual form (tathniyah) serves to display the complete care taken in creating him, peace be upon him, which calls for honouring and magnifying him, with the aim of emphasising the denunciation and intensifying the reproach.

﴿Did you act arrogantly?﴾ With the interrogative hamzah of denial and the omission of the hamzat al-wasl (the connecting hamzah); that is: did you make yourself proud without any entitlement?

﴿Or were you among the exalted?﴾ That is, those deserving of superiority. It has also been said: "Have you now become arrogant, or have you not ceased, since you existed, to be among the arrogant?" It is also recited with the omission of the interrogative hamzah, relying on the indication of "am" (or) to it. (p-237) And His Exalted saying:

"He said, 'I am better than him.'" This is his claim to something that would, in his own reckoning, prevent him from prostrating, and an indication that it is not fitting for the superior to prostrate before the inferior, as his words express: ﴿I would not prostrate to a human whom You created from clay, from black mud altered﴾. His words ﴿You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾ are a justification for what he claimed of his superiority over him (peace be upon him). The accursed one erred in restricting superiority to what pertains to the material and the element, and overlooked what pertains to the Agent, as His words ﴿for what I created with My two hands﴾ inform us, and what pertains to the form, as His words ﴿and I breathed into him of My spirit﴾ point out, and what pertains to the final purpose, which is the crux of the matter. For this reason He commanded the angels (peace be upon them) to prostrate to him when it became clear to them that he knew more than they did about that upon which the matter of the caliphate on earth turns, and that he had special qualities not possessed by anyone else.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 77:**

﴿He said, "So get out of it"﴾. The "fa'" (فاءُ, the particle of consequence) indicates that the command follows from what appeared from the accursed one of opposition to the glorious command and of justifying it with falsehoods. That is: "So get out of Paradise, or out of the company of the angels." This is what is meant by the command to descend, not descent from the heaven, as has been said. For his whispering to Adam, peace be upon him, came after this expulsion, and the manner of his whispering has been explained in Surat al-Baqarah. It has also been said: "Get out of the form in which you were, and strip yourself of it," for he used to take pride in his form, so God changed his form, and he became black after he had been white, ugly after he had been beautiful, and dark after he had been luminous.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿for you are accursed﴾, is a justification for the command to leave: that is, you are banished from every good and honor. For whoever is banished is stoned with rocks, or [it means] a devil who is stoned with shooting stars.

﴿And indeed upon you is My curse﴾, that is, My removal from mercy. Its restriction by the possessive form ("My curse"), while in His saying ﴿And indeed upon you is the curse﴾ it is unrestricted, is because the cursing by those who curse, from among the angels and the two weights (al-thaqalayn, i.e., jinn and humankind) as well, is also from His direction. They invoke upon him the curse of God Most High and his removal from mercy.

﴿Until the Day of Religion﴾, that is, the Day of Recompense and punishment. In this there is an indication that the curse, despite its complete grievousness, is not the recompense for his crime. Rather, it is a model of what he will encounter, continuing until that day. Yet this does not mean that it will end on that day, as the apparent limit of time might suggest. Rather, it means that on that day he will suffer kinds of torment and varieties of punishment that will make him forget the curse, and it will become like something that has passed. Do you not see His saying, Most High: ﴿Then a caller will call out among them: The curse of God is upon the wrongdoers﴾, and His saying, Most High: ﴿And some of you will curse others﴾?

**[Qur'an 38:79]** ﴿He said: "My Lord, then reprieve me﴾ — that is, grant me respite and delay me. The "fa" (فَ) here is connected to an omitted element that the speech implies; that is, "Since You have made me one who is stoned (rajim), then reprieve me and do not cause me to die."

﴿until the day they are resurrected﴾ — that is, Adam and his descendants, for recompense after their annihilation. By this he intended to find a breathing space for leading them astray, to take his revenge upon them, and to escape death altogether, since there is no death after the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 80:

﴿He said, "Indeed, you are among those given respite."﴾ The answer comes in a nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya), together with an allusion to the fact that what he asked for is extended to others as well, in a manner that suggests the petitioner is following them (p-238). In this there is clear evidence that it is an announcement (ikhbar) of the respite decreed for them from eternity (azalan), not a fresh granting (insha') of a particular respite that had already taken place in answer to his supplication. It also shows that his request for respite was a request to postpone death, since by it his being among them is realized, and not a request to postpone punishment, as has been said. For this is known from the idafa of "the day" to "the religion" (ila'l-din), meaning: you are among those whose terms were deferred from eternity, according to what the wisdom of creation requires.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 81:

﴿Until the Day of the Appointed Time﴾, which Allah has decreed and determined for the annihilation of creation, and it is the time of the First Blowing (al-nafkha al-ula). It is not until the time of resurrection (al-ba'th), which is the one being asked about. So the "fa'" (fa, the connecting particle) is not for linking the granting of respite itself to the request for respite, but for linking the statement mentioned with it, as in the saying of one who said:

"So if You show mercy, You are indeed worthy of it"

For it is not possible to make the fa' here link what Allah, exalted is He, has of eternal worthiness for mercy with the occurrence of a newly-occurring mercy. Rather, it links the statement of that worthiness for mercy with its occurrence. This is so. The specifying of the time has been omitted in Surah al-A'raf, just as the calling out (al-nida') and the fa' have been omitted in the request for respite and the granting of respite, relying on what has been mentioned here and in Surah al-Hijr. And if it occurs to you that every aspect of the noble composition must have a particular situation that requires it, different from the situation of others, and that what was related from the accursed one was uttered by him only once, and likewise his reply occurred only once, then the situation of the request for respite and the granting of respite, if it requires one of the aspects that have been related, then that aspect is the one that corresponds to the requirement of the situation, and the one that reaches the rank of eloquence and the degree of inimitability (i'jaz). As for the other aspects, they are far from reaching the level of eloquence, let alone ascending to the heights of inimitability. Its verification has already passed in Surah al-A'raf, by the grace and success of Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 82:

﴿Said: "Then by Your might"﴾ The "ba'" (bi-) is for oath (qasam), and the "fa'" (fa-) is for the sequential arrangement of the content of the sentence upon the granting of respite. Its statement, the Exalted: ﴿"Then, because You have led me astray"﴾, and His statement: ﴿"My Lord, because You have led me astray"﴾ do not contradict this, for His, the Exalted's, leading him astray is one of the effects of His, the Exalted's, power and might, and a ruling among the rulings of His dominion and sovereignty. So the import of swearing by either of them is one. Perhaps the accursed one swore by both of them together, and related his oath at one time by one of them and at another time by the other, meaning: "So I swear by Your might."

﴿"I will surely lead them astray, all of them"﴾, that is, the descendants of Adam, by adorning sins for them.

﴿Except Your sincere servants from among them﴾. These are the ones whom God, exalted is He, has purified (akhlasahumu) for His obedience and protected from misguidance. It is also recited as (al-mukhlisin), in the active form, meaning: those who made their hearts and their deeds sincere for God, exalted is He.

"He said": that is, Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿So the truth is, and the truth I speak﴾. The first ﴿al-haqq﴾ is in the nominative (marfu') as either a subject with an omitted predicate (mubtada' mahdhuf al-khabar), or a predicate with an omitted subject (khabar mahdhuf al-mubtada'). The second ﴿al-haqqa﴾ is in the accusative (mansub) as a direct object (maf'ul) of the verb that follows it, placed before it for restriction (li-l-qasr); that is, "I speak nothing but the truth." The ﴿fa﴾ (fa') indicates the sequencing of what follows it relative to what precedes it; that is, "so the truth is My oath."

﴿لأمْلأنَّ جَهَنَّمَ﴾ on the basis that al-Haqq (the Truth) is either one of God's names, the Exalted; or the opposite of falsehood, which God magnified by swearing by it; or "I am the Truth"; or "My word is the Truth." God's words ﴿لأمْلأنَّ جَهَنَّمَ﴾ . . . etc. are then the answer to an omitted oath, i.e., "By God, I shall surely fill . . ." etc. God's words ﴿والحَقَّ أقُولُ﴾ are, in every case, a (p-239) parenthetical clause. On the first two interpretations it is parenthetical to the content of the oath clause, and on the third interpretation it is parenthetical to the preceding clause, namely "My word is the Truth." They have also been read in the accusative, so that the first word is sworn by, as in your saying "By God, I will surely do," with its answer being ﴿لأمْلأنَّ﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause. They have also been read in the genitive, so that the first word is sworn by with the particle of oath omitted, as in your saying "By God, I will surely do, and the Truth I say," reproducing the wording of the one sworn by, on the assumption that it means the opposite of falsehood, and its meaning is emphasis and intensification. It has also been read with the first word in the genitive by omitting the particle of oath, and the second word in the accusative as an object.

﴿مِنكَ﴾ i.e., from your kind, of the devils.

﴿وَمِمَّنْ تَبِعَكَ﴾ in error and misguidance.

﴿مِنهُمْ﴾ and from the descendants of Adam.

﴿أجْمَعِينَ﴾ is an emphasis of the second-person pronoun (the kaf) and what is conjoined to it, i.e., "I shall surely fill it with those who were followed and with the followers, all of them." Like God's words ﴿لَمَن تَبِعَكَ مِنهم لأمْلأنَّ جَهَنَّمَ مِنكم أجْمَعِينَ﴾ (Whoever among them follows you, I will surely fill Hell with you all). This statement is what is meant by God's words ﴿وَلَكِنْ حَقَّ القَوْلُ مِنِّي لأمْلأنَّ جَهَنَّمَ مِنَ الجِنَّةِ والنّاسِ أجْمَعِينَ﴾ (But the word from Me has come true: I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men, all of them). Since the basis of the ruling here is the following of Satan, it becomes clear that the basis of the absence of divine will in God's words ﴿وَلَوْ شِئْنا لآتَيْنا كُلَّ نَفْسٍ هُداها﴾ (Had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance) is the unbelievers' following of Satan through their own evil choice, not the realization of the word. So there is no trace of compulsion in this, so reflect.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 86:

﴿Say: I do not ask you any wage for it﴾ — for the Qur'an, or for conveying what is revealed to me — ﴿any reward﴾ of a worldly kind, ﴿nor am I of those who pretend﴾, that is, those who affect what is not within their nature, so that I would claim prophethood and fabricate the Qur'an.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 87:

﴿Innahu huwa﴾, that is: it is not other than.

﴿Illa dhikrun﴾ from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿for the worlds﴾, that is: for both the two weights (al-thaqalan, i.e. humankind and jinn) entirely.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 38, verse 88:**

﴿And you will surely come to know its news﴾ That is: what it informed of, namely the promise and the warning and other things, or the truth of its report and that it is the truth and the reality.

﴿After a while﴾ After death. Or on the Day of Resurrection. Or at the appearance and spread of Islam. It was also said: whoever remains will know it when its matter becomes manifest and prevails, and whoever dies will know it after death. There is in this a threat that is not hidden.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): ﴿Whoever recites Surah Sad, he will have for him, by the weight of every mountain that Allah subjected to Dawud, ten good deeds, and he will be protected from persisting in a sin, small or great.﴾ Abu Umamah said: Allah the Exalted protected him from every sin, small or great. And Allah knows best.
